extracted.intended_audience: general readers, naturalists, and scientists interested in evolution and species theory
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining and evaluating Darwin's Origin of Species for a non-specialist but scientifically literate audience; distinguishing facts from theory and assessing scientific logic in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreter's duties (distinguish facts vs theory; test scientific logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: To point out the nature of the problems which it discusses; to distinguish between the ascertained facts and the theoretical views which it contains; and finally, to show the extent to which the explanation it offers satisfies the requirements of scientific logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When summarizing or interpreting a major scientific work: separate empirical, established facts from hypotheses and theoretical constructions; explicitly evaluate how well the proposed explanation meets standards of scientific logic. Use this as the organising aim of exposition for non-specialist readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and obvious logical bond (avoid 'pemmican' compression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding the clearness of the style, those who attempt fairly to digest the book find much of it a sort of intellectual pemmican--a mass of facts crushed and pounded into shape, rather than held together by the ordinary medium of an obvious logical bond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overload exposition with densely packed facts without making the connecting logic explicit. Writers should reveal the logical structure linking evidence to conclusions rather than assuming readers will supply missing connective reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient evidence; avoid gratuitous assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: From sheer want of room, much has to be taken for granted which might readily enough be proved; and hence, while the adept ... discovers fresh proof ... the novice in biology is apt to complain of the frequency of what he fancies is gratuitous assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid leaving essential steps implicit. Where possible, supply or signpost proofs, examples, or accessible demonstrations for claims that non-expert readers cannot be expected to fill in from prior knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological species definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarded from the former point of view, a species is nothing more than a kind of animal or plant, which is distinctly definable from all others, by certain constant, and not merely sexual, morphological peculiarities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constant, non-sexual structural characters to delimit species when only morphological evidence (skins, bones, fossils) is available. Emphasize diagnostic features that are consistently present across individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological species definition (descent-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most physiologists consider species to be definable as 'the offspring of a single primitive stock.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, adopt a definition of species based on common descent/lineage (physiological species), but be explicit about the assumptions (e.g., 'primitive' stock) and empirical limits of applying this definition in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological versus physiological distinction and conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: The following out of the properties exhibited by physiological species would lead us into difficulties ... the physiological definition of species is likely to clash with the morphological definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that morphological distinctness does not always equal separate lineage; explicitly discuss which concept of species is being used and the implications for classification and interpretation of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybridization/fertility as a test for physiological species
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual answer of physiologists is in the affirmative. It is said that such a test is to be found in the phenomena of hybridization--in the results of crossing races, as compared with the results of crossing species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interbreeding and fertility of hybrids as a criterion to infer common physiological species when practical, but treat results as empirical evidence subject to caveats (see limitations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and caveats of the hybridization test
rubrics_metrics.description: The test would be an admirable one, if, in the first place, it were always practicable to apply it, and if, in the second, it always yielded results susceptible of a definite interpretation. Unfortunately, in the great majority of cases, this touchstone for species is wholly inapplicable... The sterility is innately variable in individuals of the same species, and is eminently susceptible of favourable and unfavourable conditions... It is generally different and sometimes widely different, in reciprocal crosses between the same two species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing hybridization/fertility tests, consider practical obstacles (wild animals not breeding in captivity, plant hermaphroditism, long-term experiments), biological variability (reciprocal crosses may differ), and environmental effects on fertility. Treat sterility/fertility as probabilistic, not definitive, evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that varieties may arise 'spontaneously' or from external influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties then arise we know not why; and it is more than probable that the majority of varieties have arisen in this 'spontaneous' manner, though ... they may be traced, in some cases, to distinct external influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In explanations of variation, acknowledge multiple causes: spontaneous (internal) variation and external (environmental) influences. Avoid simplistic attributions of variation solely to environmental adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heritability and pre-potency of varieties (selection relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once in existence, varieties obey the fundamental law of reproduction that like tends to produce like; and their offspring exemplify it by tending to exhibit the same deviation from the parental stock as themselves... there seems to be, in many instances, a pre-potent influence about a newly-arisen variety which gives it ... an unfair advantage over the normal descendants from the same stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a variation can found a race, evaluate its heritability and any evidence of 'pre-potency' (tendency to reproduce itself strongly). Use pedigree and breeding data to judge transmissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of both parents to establish a race (breeding true)
rubrics_metrics.description: A race is a propagated variety; and as, by the laws of reproduction, offspring tend to assume the parental forms, they will be more likely to propagate a variation exhibited by both parents than that possessed by only one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish a breed/race from a variant, select breeding stock from both sexes that exhibit the trait; long-term selection across generations is required to fix the trait and produce 'breeding true' lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of variation and potential for endless raciation under selection
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no organ of the body of an animal which may not, and does not, occasionally, vary more or less from the normal type; and there is no variation which may not be transmitted and which, if selectively transmitted, may not become the foundation of a race... new races may be developed out of the pre-existing one 'ad infinitum', or, at least, within any limit at present determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the potential for variation in any trait and the cumulative effect of selective breeding; when theorizing about diversification, allow for extensive divergence given sufficient time and selection pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of controlled pedigree/breeding examples to support theoretical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as the Ancon sheep and Gratio Kelleia's hexadactyl descendants illustrate how selection and mating patterns affect whether a variation becomes a race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support theoretical arguments about origin of races with concrete breeding histories and pedigrees; examine mating patterns (e.g., assortative mating, inbreeding) to explain why some variants persist and others do not.
